content: Thiabutenes are a class of opioid analgesic drugs. The parent compound, thiambutene, itself does not exhibit analgesic effects. However, several derivatives within this group possess analgesic properties comparable in potency to morphine. Notable compounds in this family include dimethylthiambutene, diethylthiambutene, ethylmethylthiambutene, pyrrolidinylthiambutene, and piperidylthiambutene. These compounds generally exhibit similar potency to morphine. Among these, diethylthiambutene has been the most widely utilized, primarily in veterinary medicine. All of these compounds, with the exception of two weaker derivatives—diallylthiambutene and morpholinylthiambutene—produce anticholinergic and antihistamine side effects. Structurally, all members of this group contain a chiral center at the alpha carbon, where the R1 group is attached. This chiral center gives rise to two stereoisomers, with the dextro isomer being the more potent form in all cases, although both isomers are pharmacologically active. Three compounds from this group—diethylthiambutene, dimethylthiambutene, and ethylmethylthiambutene—are explicitly classified as illegal drugs under United Nations conventions, making them prohibited worldwide. The remaining compounds are only considered illegal in countries with laws analogous to the Federal Analog Act, such as the United States, Australia, and New Zealand.
